raw_case_text:
A 60-year-old Omani male presented to the emergency department at Sultan Qaboos University Hospital, Oman, with an acute febrile illness for four days associated with severe pain and stiffness of large and small joints, muscle and body pain, extreme fatigability, and a rash on his lower extremities. His joint pain was severe and incapacitating. The pain involved the small joints of his hands, and both wrists, shoulders, ankles, and knees. The patient had returned from a family visit to Karachi, Pakistan, one day before presentation. However, his symptoms started three days before returning to Oman. The patient was accompanied during his travel by his wife and children all of whom experienced similar symptoms while in Pakistan and spontaneously recovered. He recalled several mosquito bites while in Karachi.
The patient was previously healthy except for well-controlled diabetes mellitus. He did not seek pre-travel counseling and did not receive vaccinations or malaria chemoprophylaxis. His only medication was metformin 1.5 g twice daily.
At triaging in the emergency department, he was alert and oriented but looked exhausted. He was febrile (38.5  C) and tachycardic (110 beats/minute). His blood pressure was 120/90 mmHg, and he had a respiratory rate of 20 breaths/minute, and oxygen saturation of 98% in room air.
General examination showed no pallor, icterus, or conjunctival hemorrhages, and no palpable lymphadenopathy. He was observed to have mild stooped posture.
Skin examination revealed diffuse, erythematous, painless, non-pruritic, and non-blanchable maculopapular rash involving lower limbs and limited to both shins. Examination of the joints demonstrated tenderness with a limited range of movement and stiffness of small joints of hands, both wrists, elbows, shoulders, ankles, and knees with mild synovitis of the left knee joint. The remainder of the physical examinations were normal.
Initial investigations revealed normal hematocrit (37%), platelets (227 x 109/L), and total white cell count (7.4 x 109/L) with moderate lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count of 0.7 x 109/L). His coagulation screen was normal. Hepatic function panel showed a two-fold rise in alanine aminotransferase (83 U/L) with normal aspartate aminotransferase (43 U/L), albumin (39 g/L), and bilirubin (6 micromol/L). His renal function and electrolytes panel were normal. Rapid antigen detection test for malaria was negative, blood culture was negative, and chest X-ray was normal. Cardiac electrocardiography was normal with the exception of sinus tachycardia.
RT-PCR for chikungunya was performed at national reference public health laboratory on patient's blood sample. This test was positive (with high chikungunya viral load) confirming acute chikungunya at the time of hospitalization. RT-PCR for dengue virus was negative.
A diagnosis of a confirmed case of travel-related chikungunya with acute polyarthralgia/polyarthritis was made. The patient was managed with simple analgesics (acetaminophen 1 g six hourly) and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (celecoxib 200 mg 12 hourly). This approach provided symptom relief with marked clinical improvement within three days. Two weeks later, the patient continued to have mild residual arthralgia (mainly left knee). However, he was able to ambulate independently but with residual mild stooped gait. Follow-up was arranged to monitor for development of post-chikungunya chronic rheumatologic disorder.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 60-year-old Omani male presented with a 4-day history of acute fever, incapacitating polyarthralgia and joint stiffness, myalgia, extreme fatigue, and a lower extremity rash after returning from Karachi, Pakistan.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three days before returning to Oman from a family visit in Karachi, Pakistan (4 days prior to emergency department presentation), the patient developed acute fever, severe incapacitating pain and stiffness in large and small joints (hands, wrists, shoulders, ankles, and knees), generalized muscle and body aches, extreme fatigability, and a lower limb rash. He recalled multiple mosquito bites in Karachi, and his accompanying wife and children experienced similar self-limiting symptoms during the trip.
subjective.past_medical_history: Well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus. Recent family travel to Karachi, Pakistan, with multiple mosquito bites and similarly affected household contacts; no pre-travel counseling, vaccinations, or malaria chemoprophylaxis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, severe large and small joint pain and stiffness, myalgia, extreme fatigue, and non-pruritic painless shin rash. Home medication: metformin 1.5 g twice daily.

objective.physical_examination: Alert and oriented but appeared exhausted, walking with a mild stooped posture. Vital signs: temperature 38.5 C, heart rate 110 beats/min, blood pressure 120/90 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. No pallor, icterus, conjunctival hemorrhage, or palpable lymphadenopathy. Skin exam: diffuse erythematous, painless, non-pruritic, non-blanchable maculopapular rash limited to both shins. Musculoskeletal exam: tenderness, stiffness, and limited range of motion across the small joints of the hands, bilateral wrists, elbows, shoulders, ankles, and knees, with mild left knee synovitis. Remainder of systemic examination was normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: hematocrit 37%, platelets 227 x 10^9/L, total WBC 7.4 x 10^9/L, with moderate lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 0.7 x 10^9/L). Coagulation screen: normal. Liver function panel: ALT elevated 2-fold at 83 U/L, AST 43 U/L (normal), albumin 39 g/L (normal), bilirubin 6 umol/L (normal). Renal function and electrolytes: normal. Malaria rapid antigen test: negative. Blood culture: negative. Chest X-ray: normal. ECG: sinus tachycardia, otherwise normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Travel-associated acute chikungunya fever with acute symmetric polyarthralgia/polyarthritis. Malaria, dengue fever, and bacteremia were excluded. Confirmation: Blood RT-PCR positive for chikungunya virus (with high viral load) at the national reference laboratory, and RT-PCR negative for dengue virus. Management and outcome: Treated with oral acetaminophen (1 g every 6 hours) and celecoxib (200 mg every 12 hours), achieving marked clinical improvement within 3 days. At 2-week follow-up, he was ambulating independently with a mild stooped gait and mild residual left knee arthralgia, with ongoing outpatient monitoring for chronic post-chikungunya rheumatism.
